why: No hyperscaler has cut 2027 plans, but cracks are showing. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo says Google is cutting 2027 shipments of a Broadcom-designed AI chip by about a fifth (neither company has commented), and Alphabet sold bonds at wider spreads than in May. After the Democratic sweep, UBS says ~30% of expected 2028 US data-centre additions could be at risk from construction pauses. Spending is still debt-funded, with free cash flow negative at three of the four biggest spenders.

Chip stocks led a sharp rebound: the chip index jumped 4.7% on Friday and the SMH chip fund rose 10% for the week, with Micron +7.6% and Broadcom +3.8% on Friday. Nvidia lagged at +0.8% to US$150.49, still about 30% below a month ago. Its board investigation and a congressional probe continue, Reuters has reported SEC staff are examining possible accounting issues (no finding of wrongdoing), and S&P Global Ratings has its AA rating on watch for a downgrade over governance.

October PCE inflation rose to 3.8% a year (core 3.3%) and Q3 growth was revised up to 4.3%, so a 25 bp hike on 9 Dec is about 97–99% priced, with another expected in January or early 2027 (26–27 Nov). US November jobs data land at 12:30am Saturday 5 Dec Melbourne time; the Fed decides at 6am Thursday 10 Dec.

No dated default-swap figures since Friday 20 Nov, when Oracle’s protection was about 328 bp (above the 300 bp bursting threshold) and CoreWeave’s about 1,233 bp. A 25 Nov report cited records of 356 bp for Oracle and 1,314 bp for CoreWeave, and SoftBank at 501 bp, without dates. Shares recovered over the week: Oracle about +5%, CoreWeave about +12%.

Anthropic jumped about 11% to US$91.88 on Friday, about 11% above its US$83 IPO price, after a weak first week of trading. Analysts have cited its capital needs and lack of a credit rating so far. No new OpenAI funding news. Nvidia’s US$118bn of customer guarantees, about US$105bn tied to one OpenAI campus, remains in focus. (Disclosure: Claude is made by Anthropic.)

About 4.90% on Friday in a shortened session, up roughly 3–5 bp as money moved back into stocks. Yields and stocks rose together, the opposite of the bursting pattern (yields falling sharply while stocks fall).

WTI settled at US$83.08 on Friday (−0.9% for the week) while Brent ended at US$95.44, up about 3% for the week on attacks on tankers and Saudi facilities. OPEC+ meets Sunday and is expected to hold output. Oil remains well above pre-war levels, keeping inflation pressure on the Fed.

The high-yield spread widened to 377 bp on 25 Nov from 323 bp on 13 Nov, so the AI sell-off has reached broad credit, though spreads are still far from crisis levels and Friday’s rally is not yet in the data. IMF: US bank loans to non-bank lenders rose 18% in 2026.

Friday’s rally was broad: the S&P 500 rose 1.6% (+5.6% for the week), the Dow 1.2%, and small caps about 6.5% for the week. The equal-weight S&P 500 fund rose 1.2% on Friday, a little behind the cap-weighted index, as tech led. Systematic funds sold about US$70bn of global shares last week and Goldman’s desk says they may sell more.
